title: Americans May Eat More Processed Food than They Think
paragraphs: Many people try to avoid ultra-processed foods, which are often linked to poor health. However, a new survey suggests that many Americans may be eating far more of these foods than they realize.
The survey was carried out by Talker Research in September 2026 for Amy's Kitchen, a company that sells frozen and canned foods. It asked 2,000 Americans about their eating habits.

On average, the respondents estimated that only 16% of their diet consisted of ultra-processed foods. However, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), these foods actually make up about 53% of the average American's diet. In other words, people may be underestimating how much ultra-processed food they eat by more than three times.

One reason may be that people find it difficult to recognize these foods. Only 9% of respondents were able to correctly identify which foods are considered ultra-processed. Many did not realize that common foods such as sliced bread, breakfast cereal, deli meat and crackers are ultra-processed. On the other hand, many people believed that plant-based milks, protein bars and granola bars were "safe" choices, even though these products often undergo heavy processing.

At the same time, some people made the opposite mistake. For example, half of the respondents thought that pasteurized milk was processed, and 40% said the same about rolled oats. In addition, 37% believed that any kind of processing automatically makes food bad for you. Half of the respondents said they were not confident that they could tell the difference between processed and ultra-processed foods, and 44% said they felt overwhelmed by conflicting information about nutrition.

Despite this confusion, many Americans are thinking about the issue. Around 71% said they think about how much ultra-processed food is in their diet. However, 61% believed that these foods are now so common that they could not avoid them even if they tried.
It is worth noting that the survey was commissioned by a food company, and the 16% figure is based on people's own estimates rather than measurements of what they actually ate.
